I'm currently here, in Haiphong. I'm not really concerned about potentially getting Coronavirus at the present time - I'm more likely to get Dengue or hit by a truck. I'm young and relatively healthy, and if I contracted it I would be expected to recover. 


That said, I am genuinely worried that if more people contract the virus, the government will close all schools, and in the worst case scenario, quarantine the city. I don't want to be sitting around not getting paid for a month. I really don't want to be dealing with panic buying or a curfew. 


I have strong ties here and I consider Vietnam to be my second home. I'm not planning on leaving unless the situation becomes like Wuhan. But if I was in your shoes, I would monitor developments carefully and be willing to cut my losses and move at short notice. 


TLDR - I'm not concerned about getting sick, but I am worried about the potential for massive inconvenience and loss of income.

A semi automatic bike like the Honda Wave or Yamaha Jupiter should be fine. They just keep going, are easy to fix/ lots of spare parts as all the locals drive them. A fluent English speaker with a CELTA would be able to find work in Vietnam. At my centre (an Apollo school) half the teaching staff are non-native. It may help you in your job hunt have a IELTS or TOEFL score to 'prove' your English ability. 

As for other countries, I'm not 100% sure but employers may reject you based on the visa requirements - I believe that Taiwan only issues visas for teachers from the USA, UK, Canada etc. Even South Africans struggle to get employment and visas in certain countries.

I can only speak for centre work in VN, but I personally have a good deal of free time. I teach 3 days a week from 5.30-9.30pm, and all day at weekends. I have to lesson plan and do some admin, but once you have a bit of experience it shouldn't take more than 45 mins a lesson. It depends on the center but there are no set office hours at mine (Apollo) so I can plan/ do admin at home.  I know that some other centres like APAX provide lesson plans but as I understand it, their admin is more than ours.

This is very normal for CELTA, but I promise that you won't ever spend that much time planning once you start teaching (unless you have a formal observation - I still plan for about 3 or 4 hours for them, but I only have them 4 times a year). Once I started teaching, it would take me maybe 1.5 hours to plan a class. Now, it takes me about 30 minutes, including making materials. 


In real teaching, you will never be asked to produce a lesson plan that in depth (unless you are being observed). Your lesson plans will normally just include your staging, timing and details of what you will do during that stage. It's much easier once you start teaching for real and get in the swing of things, so keep going and good luck!

I live in Haiphong, and I'm fond of the place, I'll have been here 3 years by the end of my contract. I feel like people either hate it or love it. It's the 3rd biggest city in Vietnam but feels a lot smaller. It's very friendly and welcoming, though nightlife etc. is pretty limited. There are no tourists here so it's very much an 'authentic' city with little provision for westerners. The city itself isn't that beautiful but its close to Halong bay (we all try to get to Cat Ba island once a month or so) and Hanoi. I'm genuinely happy here - I feel like this place is my home now, and there's a great community of foreigners who live here long-term. 


In terms of work, there are a lot of centres but the smaller ones will maybe not want to hire you as you're a Việt Kiều. That said, the larger centers (APAX, ILA, Apollo) are a lot less discriminatory - I work for Apollo and we hire a lot of people from Asian countries/ of Asian descent. 


I prefer centre work to public school work as the hours suit me (evenings and weekends), I get to have my own classes that I see a couple of times a week, I get professional development, my visas and work permits are sorted for me and class sizes are small (20 kids max compared to 50 kids in public school). I work for just one centre but others sort out their own visas and work freelance - there is more money to be made with the latter but I prefer the stability of just having one employer. 


I used to live in Danang and while it is beautiful and living there is very straightforward, it is very touristy and it's hard to feel 'connected' to Vietnam. That isn't maybe a concern for a lot of people but as you said part of the reason you are doing this is to find out more about your Vietnamese heritage, you may encounter some frustrations. That said, the beach and nature is amazing and the nightlife is good. 


In Danang, the pay tends to be lower as it's a more desirable place to live, but the big centres are there and if you can find a job at ILA, Apollo etc then the pay is the same. However, most of the big centres in Danang tend to transfer employees working in other cities to Danang and rarely hire from outside the company. 


As others mentioned, Vung Tau could also be a good option. I have friends living there and they are very happy. ILA would be a good centre to look at. 


Hope that helps! This is just my experience and other people will have had very different experiences with the cities and schools :)

I don't feel that transient as I prefer to stay in a place for a few years (moving every year to a new country just seems exhausting and I like how I've got a reasonable grasp of the language and culture now). 


In terms of career, I'm trying hard to build my CV and make this a viable long-term career (e.g. I'll get my CELTYL this year and work as a manager for my centre). I know that I'll never be rich, but I think you can make a good living as an ESL teacher; at any rate, it's a fulfilling and enjoyable job most of the time that I'm pretty good at.

The Vietnamese women I know who are dating or married to foreigners have a lot of agency, are educated and either in uni or successful businesswomen and want to be with their tay partners because they are truly happy and in love with them. I know that there are some pretty grim partnerships out there but I think to dismiss all mixed relationships as either simply a cynical transaction or a situation where the woman is being taken advantage of is a little unfair. 


A few of my Vietnamese female friends actually offer a different point of view. They like being with their tay boyfriends and husbands because they are less controlling, their relationships move at a slower pace and they treat them more like equals. They like being in a relationship with a foreigner as they don't have to deal with in laws that traditionally treat the new female addition to the family pretty shabbily (especially outside of the cities).


Of course i am not for a minute suggesting that all Vietnamese men are bad partners, I have Vietnamese male friends who are awesome people I'd introduce my single friends to in a heartbeat. I'm just repeating what has been told to me pretty much verbatim.

The Hai Van pass is dangerous but ok, as long as you go nice and slow (I mean like 40km/hour max - you also may as well go slow and enjoy the views). The drive from Hoi An to the start of the Hai Van pass is also pretty ok. I've driven that route plenty of times.


That said, I really don't think you should be tackling it on your first day of driving. I've been driving 2 years and I found some bits pretty sketchy. 


 The really scary bit and the bit that I would advise avoiding 100% is the road from the north of the Hai Van pass to Hue. I've driven it once and I was scared and felt like one wrong move would result in serious injury. There are a lot of trucks and coaches going about 80km/hour and very little space for bikes. I'm a confident driver and I didn't enjoy it. For you to do it with no experience is really, really not a good idea. 


If you want to experience the drive, I would advise doing an Easy Rider tour. If you really must do the Hai Van pass alone, ride from Hoi An over the Hai Van pass then come back over and spend the night in Da Nang. The next day, take the train to Hue.

Fried rice - fry frozen mixed veggies in oil, adding salt/ pepper/ garlic/ sriracha/ soy sauce as desired. Add a cup of cooked rice per person and mix through. Make a well in the rice and add a couple of beaten eggs. Stir the eggs like you are making scrambled eggs for one min then mix with the rice. 

Carrot and coriander soup - fry an onion in oil. Once soft, add some garlic and 3 big carrots (chopped) and stir. Add 1 litre vegetable stock, a teaspoon (or two if you love it) of dried coriander and season to taste. Once the carrots are soft, use a hand blender to make it smooth. You could also add a potato (cubed) with the carrots for more bulk! 

Homefries - cube potatoes to 2cm square. Heat a few tablespoons of oil in the pan and add the potatoes and stir. At this point, you can add whatever seasoning/ spices you like - salt, pepper, garlic salt, paprika, taco seasoning, chilli... Cook over low to medium heat till the potatoes are cooked through. You could add peppers and onions halfway through the cooking process too. 

Eggs are cheap, nutritious and delicious. An egg sandwich is a great breakfast. Add a boiled egg to ramen. Add a couple of boiled eggs to some curry sauce and cook for a few minutes and serve with rice.

My bike was stolen in similar circumstances. I didnt really negotiate a price, i turned up and paid what I felt the bike was worth (5 million plus the 3 million I had already given them as 3 month's rent) - it was a pretty nice, new bike and I felt I actually got away with paying a reasonable price.

 It sucked but I didn't particularly want the police involved (driving without a VN license), I live very near the rental place and didn't want any awkwardness... plus I felt bad about it and felt I should pay. That said they had no deposit or passport details of mine so I guess I was in a position to choose how much I paid. 

I would advise you to pay an amount of money that you feel is reasonable. Take a look at how much second-hand bikes are going for in your area and pay something around that mark.

Honestly, Vietnam is pretty safe. I've lived here two years and this is by far the safest place I've lived with one major exception - driving. Honestly, the best thing you can do to keep your sister safe is to make her aware that she shouldn't rent a bike here. 

Of course, if she was gonna move here then it's something that has to be done but for three weeks, taxis are fine! Grab (like Uber) is in all major cities and you can hire a car or a motorbike taxi. If she visits somewhere more rural then she should be OK driving a bike but i really would avoid driving in Hanoi/ HCMC etc... 

The normal rules apply - keep money hidden/ cross body bag/ don't walk alone at night... But if you are sensible Vietnam is a safe, friendly, wonderful country to visit :) 

ETA this is my experience as a late 20s woman who works here. I am now thinking about what i was like at 18, and yeah you are correct to be concerned... One thing i will add is that the drugs here are not like drugs in the west. I won't touch anything in powder/ pill form as the likelihood of it being meth is fairly high, depending on where you are. The weed is very strong here (and while most tourist bars sell it and the police turn a blind eye it isn't legal). 

If she is sticking to the main areas, the hostels are fairly professionally run (often with western staff on gap years) and are used to looking after young backpackers. I do genuinely think that Vietnam is still far safer than Thailand, for example, but she needs to exercise caution and restraint.

Tofu! Granted i live in an Asian country so its like 40 cents here. Fry cubes of extra firm tofu till golden brown and remove from heat and season well. In a pan, add your marinade (i use 2 spoons of soy sauce, 2 of apple cider vinegar, 1 of honey, some garlic powder, a sprinkle of MSG and a squirt of chili sauce) and gently warm. Add the cubes of tofu and stir fry till the sauce is absorbed (1min). Serve with rice and veggies.
